title: Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets
research_question: Can risk-controlling prediction sets be extended to sequential and actively labeled data so that risk control remains valid at every stopping time while labels are acquired efficiently under a budget?
methodology: The paper builds anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets using betting-based e-processes, yielding a time-uniform guarantee over the entire sequential process rather than a guarantee only at a predetermined sample size. It extends the construction to adaptive label acquisition through randomized labeling policies and inverse-propensity correction, and adds a learned conditional-risk predictor as a variance-reduction control variate. The authors analytically characterize optimal predictors and label-allocation policies under a labeling budget and derive regret results relating estimation error to e-process growth. Numerical simulations and ImageNet experiments compare label-all, oblivious random sampling, pretrained, and online-learned active policies.

key_findings.finding: The paper establishes an anytime-valid risk-control guarantee that holds simultaneously over all time steps, allowing the procedure to be stopped adaptively without invalidating the stated risk guarantee under its assumptions.
Adaptive label sampling with inverse-propensity correction preserves the validity of the e-process construction while allowing the expected labeling rate to be constrained by a budget.

The theoretically optimal auxiliary predictor is the conditional expected risk given the features, and the optimal labeling probability is related to the conditional residual variability under the budget constraint.

Prediction error and deviation of the learned sampling policy from the optimal policy reduce expected wealth growth and therefore statistical efficiency, with this loss characterized by the paper's regret analysis.

In both the numerical simulations and ImageNet experiments, the pretrained and learned active policies reach better prediction-set utility for a given number of queried labels than the label-all and oblivious strategies while the observed safety-violation rate remains below the configured level.

limitations: The central theoretical development primarily assumes i.i.d. data, and the authors explicitly identify test-time distribution shift as an unresolved extension.
The theory uses a lower-bounded labeling policy and an existence assumption for the analytically optimal sampling policy.
Empirical validation is limited to simulations and ImageNet rather than retrieval, language generation, or evidence-adjudication systems.
The method controls a mathematically specified prediction risk; it does not itself define how free-form evidence completeness or omission risk should be measured.
The framework does not model temporal document versions, source provenance, or permission-aware retrieval.
Applying the guarantees to adaptive RAG would require defining an appropriate bounded loss and justifying how retrieval-induced non-i.i.d. dependence fits the statistical assumptions.
raw_claims: The proposed RCPS guarantee is time-uniform rather than valid only at one fixed sample size.
The construction uses nonnegative betting e-processes and Ville-type maximal inequalities.
Labels may be queried adaptively according to probabilities that depend on the observed feature vector.
Inverse-propensity weighting corrects for selective label acquisition.
An auxiliary prediction of conditional risk is used to reduce variance without being required for validity.
The optimal auxiliary predictor equals the conditional expectation of the risk given the observed features.
The optimal sampling rule allocates more labeling probability where residual risk variability is larger, subject to the budget.
The empirical study compares active policies with labeling every example and with oblivious random labeling.
Pretrained and learned policies are more label-efficient in the reported simulation and ImageNet studies.
The authors identify distribution shift as a major direction not covered by the primary i.i.d. analysis.
